text: Good afternoon to all of you. We're going to be waiting for the ranking member to arrive, and then we'll start this hearing. All right, so the Subcommittee on the Western Hemisphere will come to order. The purpose of this hearing is to examine the threats to free and fair elections in Honduras under the Xiomara Castro government and to highlight how the United States can ensure that the will of the Honduran people is honored and respected on November 30th. I now recognize myself for an opening statement, a statement that I'm going to pronounce in English and in Spanish. I know that this hearing is being broadcast to Honduras, so I want to give the benefit of the Hondurans to understand what I'm going to say in English, also in Spanish. On November 30th, Honduras will not just pick a new president, it will choose its political destiny for the next century. It is the responsibility of the United States government and this committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee of the United States Congress, to ensure that in Honduras, freedom and democracy will prevail. Four years ago, the people of Honduras elected a socialist president called Xiomara Castro. Madam Castro has been a loyal follower, in her own words, of Fidel Castro in Cuba and Hugo Chávez in Venezuela. Do I have to explain to this audience what those two murderers did to their countries? Maybe not, because everybody knows. Unfortunately, and because of that poisonous ideology that the current president has embraced, Madam Castro has pushed her country into an economic abyss. And why do I say that? You can keep the door closed, please. Thank you. Thank you. And why do I say that? First, President Castro welcomed communist China and even suggested that she may give Palmerola Air Base to the Chinese. The Palmerola base is the key United States military installation in Latin America. Second, she broke relations with democratic Taiwan just to please China. Third, she gave another thug called Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela the highest Medal of Honor that the country can give to a civilian, the Order of Francisco Morazán. I am sure that Morazán has to be rolling in his grave. And fourth, flooded the country with Cuban spies dressed as doctors, teachers, and psychologists. 10 days from today—10 days from today, the fate of Honduras is in the hands of three candidates: Papi a la Orden, whose real name is Nasry Asfura, Salvador Nasralla, and Rixi Moncada. Mrs. Moncada is the heir to the communist throne picked by the current president. Mrs. Moncada says that Cuba is a democracy and that she wants Honduras to look just like Cuba. Well, this is the way Cuba looks today. I'm sure that Hondurans would not want that in their streets. At this hour, the voters of Honduras are at a crossroads, and they should think long and hard who are they going to vote for. As the chairwoman of the Western Hemisphere Subcommittee within the House Foreign Affairs Committee of the United States Congress, I am not telling you who to vote for. All I am saying is, do not elect a communist. Communism is beautiful in theory and miserable in practice. Look at Venezuela. After 25 years—or 25 years ago, the Venezuelans were oblivious to the same warning I am saying today, and not even having the largest reserves of oil in the world saved them from the economic catastrophe they're living today. Socialism's number one goal is to corrode the democratic institutional—institutions, especially the armed forces. The Honduran armed forces, the most powerful institution in the country, are demanding direct access to private voter information. The armed forces are demanding to know who voted for who. This is not the military which has made Hondurans proud for over 100 years. At the same time, or the same military, I should say, that pulled Mel Zelaya, the husband of the current president, out of his bed in his PJs, sent him to Costa Rica in the middle of the night for wanting to do the same thing that his wife is trying to do right now, impose communism in Honduras. 16 years ago, the military saved their country from communism, and today they need to do the same thing. So this committee is sending a very clear message, supported by the State Department and the Trump administration, that Honduras must hold a free, fair, and transparent elections. No intimidation, no stolen ballots, no foreign interference. The eye of the United States is upon Honduras this November 30th. In the United States, there are more than 1 million Hondurans, hundreds of thousands of them in my own district, Florida District number 27, the heart of the city of Miami. Oh, I know Hondurans very well. They are good people, hardworking, God-fearing, law-abiding, who have been beaten by a political class that has not treated them well for decades. They deserve someone who is not a communist, who will put the future of Honduras first, and that includes the two right candidates as well. Whomever wins these elections needs to put the fatherland above their own personal interests. Honduras's political class admires the American political and economic system. Well, it's time for them to start copying it. The nation's treasury is not their own personal checking account. The well-being of the average Honduran should be their only interest. Honduras deserves better. May the Lord guide them this November 30th. So those are my remarks in English. I am so sorry, I'm going to have to say the same remarks in Spanish for those who are watching and those who are not present in this room. And then I will give my colleagues time to ask their questions. El próximo 30 de noviembre, Honduras no solamente va a elegir a un presidente, sino va a decidir si la nación va a seguir siendo libre o no, o si cae en las garras del comunismo. Ese día, el país no va a votar por un nombre, va a votar por un futuro. Y la responsabilidad del gobierno de los Estados Unidos y de este comité y del Comité de Asuntos Exteriores del Congreso es velar porque en Honduras prevalezca la libertad y la democracia. Hace cuatro años el pueblo hondureño eligió a una presidenta socialista que se llama Xiomara Castro. La señora Castro se ha declarado con sus propias palabras admiradora de Fidel Castro y de Hugo Chávez. Yo no tengo que explicar lo que esos dos señores han hecho en sus países. La miseria, el exilio y la represión hablan por sí solos. Lamentablemente,
y

gracias a esa ideología tóxica que la señora Castro ha abrazado, Honduras ha sido empujada a un abismo económico. ¿Y por qué digo eso? Bueno, primero, porque la señora Castro le abrió las puertas al régimen comunista de China y hasta ha dicho que podría entregarles la base aérea de Palmerola, que es una instalación militar estadounidense, la más importante en América Latina. Segundo, rompió relaciones con la democrática Taiwán para congraciarse con Beijing. Tercero, decoró al a otro tirano, a otro bandido, Nicolás Maduro, con la más alta distinción civil de Honduras, la Orden de Francisco Morazán. Morazán debe estar revolcándose en la tumba después que eso pasó. Y cuarto, llenó al país de espías cubanos disfrazados de médicos, maestros y psicólogos. A 10 días de las elecciones, el futuro de Honduras está en manos de tres candidatos: Papi a la Orden, cuyo nombre verdadero es Nasry Asfura, Salvador Nasralla y Rixi Moncada. La señora Moncada es la heredera del proyecto comunista seleccionado por la señora Castro. El pueblo hondureño se merece algo mejor. La señora Rixi dice que Cuba es una democracia y que quiere convertir a Honduras en el próximo paraíso caribeño. Vamos a ver cómo luce el próximo paraíso caribeño. Ese es el futuro que quieren para los hondureños. En este momento, los votantes hondureños están en una encrucijada y deben pensar muy bien por quién van a votar. Como presidenta del Subcomité del Hemisferio Occidental del Comité de Asuntos Exteriores de la Cámara de Representantes, yo no les estoy diciendo a nadie cómo tienen que votar. Lo único que le estoy diciendo es que no elijan a un comunista, porque el comunismo es fantástico en la teoría y terrible en la práctica. Si no, pregúntenle a mis padres. Los venezolanos ignoraron esta misma advertencia hace 25 años, y ni siquiera tener las mayores reservas de petróleo del planeta los han podido salvar de la catástrofe en la que vive Venezuela en este momento. Y ahora, las Fuerzas Armadas, la institución más poderosa del país, está exigiendo acceso directo a la información privada de los votantes. Pero ¿de cuándo acá los militares tienen que estar contando votos? Ese no es el mismo ejército que ha hecho que Honduras se sienta orgulloso por más de 100 años. Ese es el mismo ejército que sacó a Mel Zelaya, esposo de la actual presidenta, de la cama, de su propia cama, en el medio de la madrugada, en pijama, y lo mandó para Costa Rica porque estaba intentando hacer lo mismo que su esposa: implementar el comunismo en Honduras. En ese momento, los militares le salvaron la vida al país. Pues hoy, 16 años después, deben estar haciendo lo mismo. Por eso este comité le está enviando un mensaje contundente y claro a las Fuerzas Armadas, que hay y respaldado este mensaje por el Departamento de Estado y por la administración del presidente Donald Trump, que Honduras tiene que celebrar elecciones libres, justas y transparentes, sin intimidación, sin colectivos, sin actas robadas, sin interferencia extranjera. Los Estados Unidos tienen puesto sus ojos este próximo 30 de noviembre en Honduras. Hay más de un millón de hondureños en los Estados Unidos, y cientos de ellos viven en mi distrito, el distrito número 27 del estado de la Florida, que es el corazón de la ciudad de Miami. Gente buena, trabajadora, creyente y respetuosa de la ley que ha sufrido por una clase política que no los ha tratado bien hace mucho tiempo. Se merecen un líder que no sea comunista, que piense primero en el futuro. Quien gane estas elecciones debe poner los intereses de la patria primero, incluyendo los dos candidatos de derecha. Que Dios proteja a Honduras porque su futuro se va a decidir ahora. I now recognize the ranking member from Texas, Representative Mr. Castro, for any statement that he may have.

Thank you, Chairwoman. We are 11 months into a new Congress and a new administration, and this is the very first hearing our subcommittee is holding on the Western Hemisphere. President Trump has brought us to the brink of war with Venezuela without the consent of the people. He's carried out extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and the Eastern Pacific. He has cut off counter-narcotics cooperation with Colombia, a trusted ally. He sent hundreds to mass detention in El Salvador without any due process and now threatens strikes against Mexico. He's canceled hundreds of millions in regional programs without explanation to Congress, and all of this has occurred without any hearings at all, without transparency, and without the oversight the Constitution requires. 11 months in, we haven't even had a budget hearing where a senior administration official comes before this committee and explains priorities for Latin America, the Caribbean, and the entire region. By November of the first year when the Democrats were last in the majority, this subcommittee had held seven hearings, with the administration testifying at four of them. And Chairwoman, I know you push for the administration to provide a witness at this hearing. I strongly supported that request, and it's unacceptable that they are refusing to provide a witness for this hearing. In over a decade, actually a dozen years on this committee, I've never seen anything like this. The Republican administration is refusing to provide a hearing, a State Department witness for a Republican chairwoman. I think that's unprecedented, and it shows you the secrecy of the Trump administration. So, Chairwoman, I urge you to hold public hearings with the administration providing testimony on these serious issues in the hemisphere, and I will back up any request to come have the Trump administration testify. The American people deserve to hear what their government is doing, and this committee must exercise our oversight responsibilities. The hearing today, of course, is about Honduras, which will be holding elections in just 10 days, and I'm certainly concerned. It seems that the Honduran people's faith in their electoral institutions is at rock bottom. This is an election where the three major candidates could plausibly be within single-digit margins of each other without any runoffs. All three major candidates and their parties have made public statements that they do not trust this process, raising the possibility that they will not respect the results of the elections. Free and fair elections are the responsibility of everyone: the government, the opposition parties, the electoral authorities, the military, and the economic elite. The National Electoral Council, the entity responsible for organizing the elections, is deadlocked, under-resourced, and facing intense political pressure by both the government and opposition parties. The Honduran government declared a state of exception in 2022, restricting civil liberties and due process, and significantly restricted the ability of civil society to act freely and independently. We've also seen worrying levels of violence and intimidation against candidates, journalists, and civil society leaders across the political spectrum, which can chill participation and further undermine confidence in the election results. This is a difficult situation that Honduran officials, candidates, and civil society will have to navigate if they're to preserve their democracy. Unfortunately, the Trump administration has not met the moment. At the beginning of the year, the administration ended State Department and USAID programs that supported the rule of law and stronger electoral institutions in Honduras. Right before the critical March primary elections in Honduras, which Hondurans had serious concerns over, the administration cut funding for civil society organizations that would have provided much-needed transparency. The Trump administration has also been unwilling to raise any concerns for most of the year, finally making a statement just last— just a week ago, when Deputy Secretary Landau raised concerns. Fortunately, Hondurans in the region seem to be mobilizing. I'm glad that the OAS, the European Union, and other organizations will be sending election missions to Honduras. I urge the government to provide them with the transparency and the freedom to conduct their work, and I'm hopeful that we will see a robust civil society presence at the elections to provide much-needed transparency and hold both the government and opposition parties accountable to democratic values. I echo the OAS's recent call for the Honduran government to respect the independence of the National Electoral Council, which must conduct its work to ensure the elections are held on time. And when the elections are held, I hope that the authorities release verifiable results without delay. We should be principled in standing for democracy and the right of a people to elect their own leaders, regardless of whether the government is on the right or the left. While the United States and the international community can raise concerns and support Honduran society in advancing democratic values and norms, our role is not to pick the leaders of Honduras. And I look forward to hearing from the witnesses at this hearing.

Thank you, Ranking Member. I hardly agree with you on many of the policy issues, but I do have to agree with you what you said, and we certainly hope that the State Department witness will come to one of these hearings in the very near future. Thank you for your comments. Now, other members of the committee are reminded that opening statements may be submitted for the record. We're pleased to have a distinguished panel of witnesses before us today on this important topic. The Honorable Carlos Trujillo, former United States Ambassador to the Organization of American States, the oldest regional international organization in the world. Before that, Ambassador Trujillo served as Special Representative to the General Assembly of the United Nations, and he also served in the Florida House of Representatives for four terms. Thank you for being here, Ambassador. And Deborah Ullmer is the Regional Director of Latin America and the Caribbean Programs at the National Democratic Institute. The NDI is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization that works to promote transparent and fair elections. Mrs. Ullmer has spent over a decade living and working in Latin America on democracy issues for NDI, for Freedom House, and for the United States government. Welcome, Madam. And lastly, we have Enrique Roig, Vice President of External Affairs at Human Rights First. Mr. Roig previously worked at the State Department and USAID on Latin American issues and has testified before this committee in other capacities. This committee recognizes the importance of the issues before us and is grateful to have you here to speak today. Your full statements will be made part of the record, and I will ask you to keep your remarks to 5 minutes or less. And now I recognize Ambassador Trujillo for his opening statement. Thank you.

Thank you, Chairwoman Salazar, Ranking Member Castro, and the distinguished members of this committee. I am deeply grateful for the invitation to appear before you today to offer testimony concerning the critical matter of the upcoming elections in Honduras. When Xiomara Castro was elected president in 2021, many welcomed her as a voice of change. Unfortunately, the reality has been significantly different. She has institutionalized a government based on extreme political ideology and has repeatedly expressed an affinity for totalitarian regimes, including those of Venezuela, Cuba, and Nicaragua. As the first months of the administration progressed, concerns immediately grew regarding the direction of the new government, particularly following her decision to eliminate and sever all diplomatic ties with Taiwan and establish and recognize the Communist Party and Republic of China. She has also failed to seat the Israeli ambassador, who has been credentialed before her for over a year and a half. They've also organized groups of street thugs organized and funded by the government known as colectivos to influence episodes of tension and violence and to intimidate the election authorities and the National Congress. Several high-level officials also chose to resign due to internal disagreements or differences of opinion with their government. Among them was Edmundo Orellana, who served as Secretary of Transparency and Anti-Corruption. In the period leading up to the current elections, civil society organizations, political sectors, and observers have expressed concerns over irregularities, particularly regarding delays and obstacles in contracting of essential services for Election Day. Recently, the tensions between the executive branch and the National Electoral Council have intensified. The former president of the Electoral Council, Cossette López-Osorio, has reported receiving death threats and judicial pressure, which, according to her, were intended to force her resignation. Magistrate Ana Paola Hall has similarly conveyed in public forums that she perceives threats to her security, escalating concerns regarding a potential maneuver to replace current electoral authorities with individuals deemed to be much more aligned with the interests of the current administration. Just last February, President Xiomara Castro's government canceled the extradition agreement for narcotics trafficking and organized crime extradition to the United States. The agreement was ultimately reinstated, but I believe the question to the committee is, why would she take such an extreme measure? She's also threatened to cancel the military cooperation of the American base in Palmerola, threats that are made repeatedly and constantly at American diplomats in-country. Another sensitive point is the role of the armed forces. If we look at the historic record, their function in election has been limited to the custody and transportation of ballot boxes across the country. However, recent statements by the high command, particularly the General Roosevelt Hernández, have been interpreted by some sectors as an attempt to involve themselves in areas beyond their constitutional authority, raising concerns about their impartiality. I would also like to add the maneuvers performed within the National Congress by the leadership of Luis Redondo similarly warrant close attention and cannot be disregarded. The government of Honduras has been operating under a state of emergency since 2022. The constitutional safeguards and rights of its citizens have ultimately been suspended. Redondo used this as an opportunity to continue ordinary sessions despite more than 78 of the 128 members of Congress demanding, demanding to return to regular session. Instead, he opted to create a permanent commission composed of nine deputies aligned with his Libre party. Through this structure, interim appointments could be imposed once officials of the National Election of Electoral Council and Electoral Justice Tribunal are suspended or removed from their positions. Finally, the role of the Public Ministry has been subject of debate. Various opposition parties have alerted that the Attorney General, Johel Zelaya, the nephew of Libre candidate Rixi Moncada, has been making decisions favoring his aunt, including legally contested actions against election electoral authorities. Some officials in this environment have temporarily left the country due to fear of prosecution or death. For members of Congress and of the Trump administration, strengthening electoral transparency in Honduras is essential. Washington maintains a significant influence in the country through security operation, family ties, and deep bilateral economic cooperation. I commend the committee members for being here today and discussing this very important election. In less than 10 days, the future of one of our great allies will be decided.
Thank you, Ambassador Trujillo. I now recognize Ms. Ullmer for her opening statement.

Thank you, Chairwoman Salazar, Ranking Member Castro, and members of the Subcommittee on the Western Hemisphere. Thank you for this opportunity to address this hearing. I've worked and lived in Honduras, where I witnessed the post-election violence in 2017. As you know, NDI organized a bipartisan pre-election assessment mission when we visited the country in early August. NDI's findings and recommendations and assistance to a broad citizen observation initiative called the Observadores Electorales de Honduras inform my observations. NDI's work is currently supported by the National Endowment for Democracy. As Honduras heads to the November 30th elections in just 10 days, the stakes extend far beyond its borders. At a moment when democracy is being tested across the globe, this vote will determine more than who governs Honduras. It will shape the country's stability and influence regional security and U.S. strategic interest in Central America. A credible election in Honduras is essential to avoiding a slide into deeper political instability. The real stake lies beyond electoral disputes, which can trigger immediate unrest. The larger danger is more profound: a leadership that assumes office without a genuine mandate, weakening democratic checks, further eroding public confidence, and undermining the country's governability in lasting ways. Washington has good reason to care. Honduras is already a major point for cocaine moving from South America to the United States. Political turmoil could make this already serious problem much worse. The country is also home to Soto Cano Air Base, a key hub for U.S. military operations in Central America. And with more than 200 U.S. companies operating in Honduras, instability could put significant American investment at risk. In short, Honduras's stability matters to American security, economic interest, and the lives of thousands of families with deep ties in both countries. Yet, Hondurans face this election with deep distrust in their government, rooted in the 2009 constitutional crises that led to a coup d'état, and the 2017 presidential reelection when allegations of fraud resulted in deadly post-election violence. Recent votes have only stoked public mistrust and instability. The March general primaries were marred by failures to safeguard ballots, and significant voting delays occurred in the country's two largest cities, in Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula. Since its August mission, NDI has heard consistent concerns about undue political interference and legal pressures on the National Electoral Council and the Electoral Justice Tribunal. These actions contribute to a serious deterioration of democratic norms, as sustained attacks from other branches of government against electoral authorities deepen the risk of prolonged political crises. In this respect, the work of the National Electoral Council hinges on the cooperation of all political actors and government institutions, including the armed forces, which are constitutionally mandated not only with safeguarding the ballots or providing overall election security, but also with guaranteeing the orderly alternation of power. The Honduran people deserve credible and transparent elections in which their votes are counted accurately and their voices are respected. NDI is still hopeful that a credible and transparent election is possible. To that end, the timing of this hearing, Madam Chairwoman, is perfect. I would like to offer the following recommendations: One, that Congress should continue voicing its strong bipartisan backing for free, fair, and transparent elections in Honduras, including through public statements, letters, and continued engagement with the Honduran authorities and civil society. Two, that the United States should continue working with the Organization of American States to initiate and sustain dialogue efforts, which will be essential as the election approaches, and in the immediate aftermath when tensions may run high. Three, the United States should explicitly affirm the importance of Honduran observers and convey its strong support for their work, emphasizing that nonpartisan and independent observation is essential for public confidence in their vote. Chairwoman Salazar, Ranking Member Castro, and members of the subcommittee, thank you again for the opportunity to testify. I look forward to your questions.
Thanks to you, Mrs. Ullmer, and I now recognize Mr. Roig for his opening and last statement. Thank you.

Chairwoman Salazar, Ranking Member Castro, and distinguished members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to testify today. I'm here on behalf of Human Rights First to discuss the upcoming elections in Honduras and the ways in which recent U.S. foreign assistance decisions have impacted the ability to support electoral observation, civil society oversight, media programs, and anti-corruption efforts. As you know, Honduras enters its next electoral cycle already burdened by increased polarization, a legacy of irregular elections, and a justice system that has been hollowed out by political manipulation and organized crime infiltration. There undoubtedly is a need for increased vigilance and raising of the alarm on the Honduras election. However, the Trump administration has been relatively silent and taken a largely transactional approach to the Castro government focused mainly on deportations. According to Human Rights First's ICE Flight Monitor, the United States, from January to October 2025, carried out 353 deportation flights to Honduras, making it the second-highest deportation destination after Guatemala. The administration also pressured Honduras into signing asylum cooperative agreements that allow the U.S. to send asylum seekers there without assessing their claims. And the administration's termination of TPS for 72,000 Hondurans in September of this year has further placed even more people at risk of removal. Now, while the Trump administration has remained focused on deportations, there are other national security interests at play that require greater vigilance of the electoral process in Honduras. Fortunately, the European Union and the Organization of American States have stepped up and called for greater transparency and legitimacy of the upcoming election. Today, Honduran civil society, much to their credit, have been able to organize domestic observers. However, they have had to cobble together their effort at the last moment because the foreign assistance they depended on was terminated. If U.S. foreign assistance had not been decimated, the Honduran observers would have greater resources to ensure increased scrutiny of the elections at this critical juncture. Unfortunately, this is not just a Honduran problem. Beginning early this year, the administration froze and terminated a broad range of USAID and State Department programs, including those that have long supported election integrity, civil society resilience, and anticorruption efforts in the region, including support to independent election observers and technical assistance to electoral authorities, investigative journalism networks and fact-checking consortia that counter disinformation during elections, digital security programs that protect activists, monitors, and independent media from targeted attacks, rule of law and anticorruption initiatives that help insulate prosecutors, auditors, and judges from political interference. Now, I know that members of this committee have asked what the administration is currently doing to support these democracy and governance programs. The short answer is clearly not enough. And while the State Department has stated publicly that some of these programs continue to be administered, the reality on the ground is a very different story. The foreign assistance dismantling has terminated or halted the core program lines for democracy, civil society, and election support that this region depends on. My previous bureau, DRL, has undergone a significant structural downgrade, with its entire Western Hemisphere expertise purged and effective elimination of most of its regional programming to support critical work in Honduras. Former USAID implementers tell us they are in survival mode—unable to plan, unable to hire, unable to continue critical election integrity and anticorruption work. And the strategic messaging coming from U.S. leadership today prioritizes deportation and short-term security concerns, not the democracy, rights, and governance work that addresses the root causes driving instability. The consequences are already visible across the region: weaker civic space, diminished oversight, and far greater room for authoritarian and criminal actors to manipulate electoral processes. Now, for decades, Democrats and Republicans alike understood that investing in these democracy and governance programs is not just about values; it is about national security. Restoring and protecting these programs are critical, as we have seen in the lead-up to high-risk elections in Honduras and elsewhere in the region. It is in the strategic interest of the United States. So, thank you again for the opportunity to testify, and I look forward to your questions.

Thank you, Mr. Roig. I now recognize myself for 5 minutes of questioning. So, I think we're all on the same page. We want Honduras to have a free, fair elections November 30th, and that is the reason why we're here, and I have two questions, and I can start with you, Ambassador Trujillo, and obviously, Deborah, you can always pitch in. Is the current Castro government trying to rig the elections, yes or no? And if they are, how are they doing it? And number three, what can the United States do in order to stop that effort?

Thank you, Madam Chair. The answer is yes, and how are they doing it? If you look at the way that they've gone after the Electoral Council, the Electoral Council is composed of one member from each party. There are three major parties in Honduras. Everyone sends their representative. The Attorney General, who happens to be Rixi Moncada, one of the candidates' nephew, has decided to summon the two opposition parties to come and testify before his office. The purpose of this testimony is to present criminal charges, to ultimately disqualify them from serving in that capacity. Who will be the replacement?
What's the importance of the National Electoral Council for those that don't understand well? Why are they— the

council adjudicates the outcomes of the elections and certifies its results. And the reason it's composed of all political parties, because you want buy-in, you want finality, you want certainty. The fact that those two members are being attacked by the actual government and by the nephew of one of the opposition candidates shows you where this election is headed. Furthermore, Redondo, who controls the National Assembly, has already named the replacements. The replacements for partisan positions are not from the same party. They're hand-selected by their government in order to influence the outcome of the election.
What can the United States do at this hour, 10 days out from the election, in order to prevent any type of stealing or rigged— rigging the presidential elections? What can we do?

First, I commend you on this hearing. I think the vigilance of this committee and the private statements and influence of members of the committee— sometimes it's difficult to recognize when you're sitting in the seats that you're sitting the importance of the words that you say and how important they are in country, in Honduras, and how it gives hope to the Honduran people. The amount of people you see sitting here behind us who really their hope on saving their democracy is kind of vested in a hearing like this. The other thing is the United States government has a plethora of tools that they could use in order to apply individual sectoral pressure to individuals who violate or usurp the rule of law, who violate or usurp democracy, individuals who commit human rights violations, whether it's in a targeted sanction matter towards an individual or towards an entire institution. I think all those tools are available, and ultimately the lack of recognition for the legitimacy of these regimes. If they do steal the election and they do go down that road, how does it end? And it has to end without any credible democratic actor recognizing the legitimacy of the regime.
Deborah, if you would like to add, I have a couple of questions for you.

Sure. Thank you. I'd like to add on messages that the US and your committee is already giving through this hearing, but messages that can be amplified. That is ensuring the respect for minimum principles of election integrity, ensuring that the elections take place on the planned date, as the OAS Secretary General has said, guaranteeing that party representatives and nonpartisan citizen observers have access to polling stations and the collation centers to ensure transparency and accountability, respecting the independence of electoral institutions so that they can fulfill their mandates, publishing prompt and verifiable results, including polling station-level results, and demonstrating the unwavering respect for the will of the people. Thank you.

Mr. Roig, I'm not sure if you are—if you feel comfortable answering this question, but the armed forces—the armed forces there is one of the most respected institutions in Honduras. I just mentioned during my initial statement, in 2009, they pulled out of his bed—I was there as a journalist—in the middle of the night, in PJs, put him on a plane, and sent him to Costa Rica because Mel Zelaya wanted to implement communism in Honduras. Now, 16 years after, his wife is doing that job. Just explain to us in which way the armed forces could stop everything that the other witnesses have described.

Yes. So Madam Chairwoman, the armed forces obviously play an important role in the elections in Honduras. They are there to safeguard and ensure the transportation of election materials, and so it's going to be important to have continued vigilance over that role that they're going to be playing, and ensure that they're not further politicized, as we've seen some of the statements coming out of heads of the military, particularly against media. And so it is concerning, and that's why we have electoral observation happening on the ground to ensure that things do go smoothly and in a way that's transparent.
What I just would like to hear from three of you, why have the Honduran armed forces been involved in a way that has not been seen in the last 50 years? There were
Yeah, I would say through General Roosevelt and many others, they're much more politicized. The rank-and-file armed forces—
did that start?
that started under this administration, under Xiomara Castro.

Thank you. It happened after my term in the OAS, but they did shift and they campaigned on breaking diplomatic relationships with Taiwan in order to favor China. China's been significantly much more active, not only in Honduras, but in the region. If you look at the last 10 years, from Honduras to Panama to Dominican Republic, I'm sure I'm missing a few, but a lot of those countries have shifted their diplomatic relationships to Taiwan— from Taiwan to China. And in Honduras in particular, they've been significantly aggressive in providing intelligence and providing some communication support and providing telecom support, and also providing strengthening diplomatic ties, including multiple state trips from Honduran high-ranking officials, including the president, to Beijing.

So just to highlight again and expand on what you said there about how they had campaigned on that, tell me how that played in the elections or what— how did that contribute to the outcome of the elections?

Well, they actively campaigned in, on having more normalized relationship, and they always, they always obviously paint it as, as trade, right? This economic engine of China, we're going to have trade, it's going to help grow our economy. It's played out throughout the rest of Latin America. It's never been the case. China's really good at importing. They're really bad at purchasing exports. So I think that continues to be the case. Going forward, it'll be interesting to see if the candidates from the opposition switch to diplomatic recognition and whether they leave from Beijing back to Taipei.
And do you think the decision to make that a part of the political campaign in the election was driven by Hondurans, or was that driven by the Chinese?
I think by both. I would say the Honduran officials who accepted the challenge and the Chinese who provided the opportunity.

Okay, thank you. We're also We were pleased to see that the Deputy Secretary of State's statement last week on the upcoming Honduran elections, he echoed the concerns of the OAS. What were those concerns, and what are the concerns that you have regarding the elections, potential irregularities, and what we should be looking sure, because we do want to make sure that there are free and fair elections occurring there.

I think the poor-functioning primaries were an indicator of what's to come: the delay in the vote counting, the military's active role, the military taking possession of ballots and not having a lot of transparency for for all parties involved, including civil society. And I think going forward, it's really the role, as some of my colleagues have said on this panel, of the Electoral Commission. If they're truly allowed to be independent, I'm not saying it'll 100% change the outcome, but at least we'll have the information to verify the outcomes of the election. The question becomes whether Honduran government officials are going to allow them to fulfill their role. And the next 10 days will determine it, but it seems they're increasingly putting more and more pressure on the independence of the Electoral Council.

All right, well, thank you again to all of you for being here today. Obviously, a great topic of interest that we're following very closely in the region, and appreciate your input and testimony today. And with that, I yield back to the chair.

Thank you, Congressman Mackenzie from Pennsylvania. And we're about to wrap this up. I think that we have been able to send a very clear message to the Hondurans, those who are watching this hearing back in Honduras, Tegucigalpa, and whatever other area in the country, that regardless whether we agree or not, Democrats and Republicans, you have seen that we have not always agreed on every single topic, but we have sent a very clear message how the American democracy works. And that is exactly what we want for Honduras and for the rest of Central America. We're sending a very clear message, Republicans and Democrats from the United States House of Representatives, that we want fair, clean elections, transparent elections, and for the Hondurans to decide their future for the next for the next 4 years. With that, I thank the witnesses for their valuable testimony and the members for their questions. The members of the subcommittee may have some additional questions for the witnesses, and they could be responded in writing. Pursuant to committee rules, all members may have 5 days to submit statements, questions, or other materials for the record, subject to the length of the limitations. And I'm going to say a few words before we close, once again in Spanish, to the Hondurans who are watching this committee. Usually, this has to be done in English, but since we are talking about our very close ally in Central America, es un mensaje muy claro el que estamos enviando desde el Congreso federal. Ustedes han visto que aquí estamos demócratas y republicanos. No siempre estamos de acuerdo en lo que estamos diciendo, pero sí estamos de acuerdo en una sola cosa: que queremos que Honduras tenga un gobierno libre, democrático, y que las elecciones del próximo 30 de noviembre sean limpias y claras. With that, may the Lord help the Hondurans and Honduras. With that, this committee stands adjourned.
